🥊 Deep Research Memo (bull/bear debated)
KLA is about as close to a genuine near-monopoly as this desk sees: roughly 55% share of the process-control category, a patent and R&D-scale moat that has held for decades, and financials that prove the moat is winning — gross margin has expanded every year for four straight years (59.8% to 61.3%) and operating margin has climbed to 41.7%, exactly the opposite trend from a name like DLO that's conceding margin to competitors. Its two most relevant rivals, Applied Materials and Lam Research, largely don't compete head-on (they're on the 'make' side, KLA is on the 'inspect' side), and its true direct competitor, Onto Innovation, remains a smaller player gaining share only in a specific niche (advanced-packaging inspection). Why now: KLA just reported a record $3.66B quarter, up 15% YoY, and raised guidance citing AI infrastructure, HBM and advanced-packaging demand — the same day this dossier was written. Revenue growth accelerated to 24% YoY (FY2026) from -7% two years prior, evidence the AI-capex supercycle is real and currently accelerating, not decelerating. Valuation and expected return: at 52.4x trailing earnings and a 2.65 PEG, this is not statistically cheap the way DLO or NRDS are — the case rests on the DCF ($602.84 vs $190.80, a 68% gap) and continued double-digit growth, not on a cheap multiple or a high FCF yield (which, at 1.7%, is actually the lowest of any name in this batch). Base case ~15%/yr, bull ~25%/yr if the AI-capex cycle sustains double-digit growth through the estimate horizon. The bear case, honestly: this is a cyclical capital-equipment business trading at a rich multiple right after its best quarter ever, and it fell -7% in revenue just two years ago — the exact playbook for a painful multiple-compression episode if AI capex even just decelerates rather than reverses. My rebuttal: the moat evidence (expanding margins, ~55% category share, three genuine sources of durability) is real and getting stronger, not weaker, which is a meaningfully different setup than a story stock riding a narrative alone — and the Street's own conservative $232.82 target (vs. the $602.84 DCF) shows the market has not gotten ahead of itself the way a true bubble top usually looks. This is a valuation-timing risk on top of a genuinely durable business, not a moat that's cracking. What to watch / when to exit: watch order/booking trends over the next 1-2 quarters for the first sign of a capex pause, any escalation in China export controls, and Onto Innovation's win rate in advanced-packaging inspection specifically. A confirmed 2+ quarter booking deceleration, not just a single soft quarter, would be the trigger to trim; the moat itself would need to show margin compression (the opposite of the last four years) before this warrants an AVOID.

Business: KLA is the dominant supplier of process-control and yield-management (inspection/metrology) equipment for semiconductor fabs — tools that verify wafers are defect-free at each manufacturing step. Its Q4 FY2026 earnings call (2026-07-28/29) reported record revenue of $3.66B, up 15% YoY, and raised guidance citing AI infrastructure, leading-edge logic, HBM and advanced-packaging demand.

MOAT: WIDE — three evidenced sources (patents, switching costs, R&D scale advantage), and unlike DLO the margin trend is expanding, not compressing, which is the clearest evidence the moat is holding under competitive pressure rather than eroding moat — intangible_assets (deep patent portfolio in inspection/metrology technology accumulated over decades); switching_costs (fabs qualify process-control tools through lengthy, expensive certification cycles and rarely re-qualify a new vendor mid-node); cost_advantage (scale in R&D spend that smaller competitors cannot match, reflected in gross margin that has itself expanded every year for four straight years: 59.8% → 60.0% → 60.9% → 61.3%, FY23-FY26). Durability: 10+. Key threat: U.S./China semiconductor export-control escalation could cut off a large customer segment (China fabs); a cyclical pause in AI-driven capex spending after the current supercycle would hit orders sharply — revenue fell -7% just two years ago (FY2024), which is the single most credible evidence this business is more cyclical than the current 52x trailing multiple implies

Bull case: Near-monopoly process-control franchise riding the AI/HBM/advanced-packaging capex supercycle, reporting record results and raised guidance the same day as this review, with a real (if partially cyclical) DCF discount and margins that are expanding, not compressing — the clearest evidence on the desk that a moat is winning against competitive pressure rather than losing to it.

Bear case: The strongest case to avoid KLA now is not about the moat — it's about paying a 52x trailing / 2.65 PEG multiple at what may be the peak of an AI-capex supercycle, in a business that fell -7% in revenue just two years ago. Semicap is a lumpy, order-driven business: fabs pull forward or delay tool purchases in bursts tied to AI-capex sentiment, not steady end-demand, and the FY2024 air pocket is recent, real, first-party evidence of exactly that pattern. KLA just printed its best quarter ever and raised guidance the same day this bull case was written — a textbook "priced for perfection" setup — and the Street's own consensus target ($232.82, only 22% above the price from 8 analysts) shows sell-side analysts are not underwriting anywhere near the DCF's implied $602.84, meaning even the bulls on Wall Street don't expect the full gap to close soon. If AI capex merely decelerates (not even reverses) over the next 4-6 quarters, a stock at 52x trailing earnings and a 1.7% FCF yield has real multiple-compression risk independent of whether the long-term moat story is right.

Competitors: Onto Innovation — KLA's most direct inspection/metrology competitor, and the one gaining share in the specific sub-segment (advanced-packaging inspection) that management is citing as a current growth driver; reported to be undercutting on price in that niche, which is worth tracking since it's exactly the growth vector the bull thesis leans on. Applied Materials and Lam Research — KLA's category share in process control is roughly 55% (near-monopoly); AMAT and Lam operate on the deposition/etch ('make') side rather than the inspection ('check') side, so there is minimal direct head-to-head today, but both are increasingly bundling in-line metrology into their own tools — a slow-moving, 5-10yr disintermediation risk to KLA's stand-alone inspection franchise rather than a near-term threat. Market-share trend: KLA's process-control share (~55%) is stable to slightly up, and margins expanding every year (59.8%→61.3% gross, FY23-FY26) is the clearest evidence the moat is winning, not losing, against this competitive set — the opposite pattern from DLO. Reinvestment runway: large and well-funded (R&D scale advantage is real and hard to replicate at KLA's size). Moat durability: survives comfortably over 3-5yr; the two threats worth tracking over 5-10yr are Onto Innovation's price-share gains in advanced-packaging inspection specifically, and AMAT/Lam's slow move to bundle metrology into deposition/etch tools. (Onto/AMAT/Lam competitive positioning is web-sourced; all KLAC financials are from the FMP bundle.)

Margin of safety: +68% below DCF ($602.84 DCF vs $190.80 price) — but the Street's own $232.82 consensus target (only 22% above the price) shows analysts are not yet underwriting anywhere near the full DCF gap, which is itself informative about how much of the gap is cyclical-peak extrapolation versus a genuine multi-year underpricing.

Expected return (3–5y): Base ~15%/yr (semicap capex cycle continues at a healthy pace, buybacks continue at -1.7%/yr share count); Bull ~25%/yr (AI-driven wafer fab equipment demand — HBM, advanced packaging, leading-edge logic — sustains double-digit growth through the estimate horizon, closing the DCF gap); Bear -10 to 0%/yr (a cyclical AI-capex pause combines with a 52x trailing multiple to produce meaningful multiple compression even without a fundamental miss — this is a wider bear-case range than the original dossier's 0-5%/yr, reflecting the FY2024 precedent of a -7% revenue year). Key assumption: AI infrastructure buildout keeps driving fab equipment orders at a double-digit clip.

What would change our mind: A confirmed 2+ quarter deceleration in AI-capex-driven bookings (order growth turning negative, not just decelerating) would be the specific, falsifiable signal that the current supercycle is rolling over the way it did into the FY2024 -7% year — that would move this toward WATCH regardless of the DCF gap. A material loss of process-control share to Onto Innovation in advanced packaging over 2-3 quarters would also warrant a re-look at the moat thesis specifically.

Catalysts: Record Q4 FY2026 results and raised outlook (2026-07-28/29, same-day news); continued HBM/advanced-packaging/AI-capex demand cited explicitly by management on the earnings call.

CIO take: A genuine, small ($697M) Munger Established-tier hit — 19% ROIC, zero debt, 22% FCF yield — but the debate found the ROIC inflection rests on one strong year after three near-breakeven ones, which is the real reason this isn't a confirmed BUY yet.

Endorsed by: DeskScreener

🥊 Deep Research Memo (bull/bear debated)
NerdWallet is a genuinely small ($697M market cap), debt-free, asset-light comparison platform that the Munger Small-Cap screen correctly flags as an 'Established' hit: 19% ROIC, 22% FCF yield, and 22% revenue growth, all at 8x trailing earnings. Its moat — trusted brand content and proprietary lender-matching data, reflected in a consistently strong 90-93% gross margin across four years — is real, if narrow, and its two most direct rivals are Credit Karma (Intuit-owned, still the largest traffic share in the category) and Bankrate (Red Ventures, dominant in the highest-value mortgage/deposit queries). Why now: the company is explicitly pivoting from SEO-dependent referral traffic toward higher-margin, vertically-integrated transactions, and FY2025 was the first year that pivot showed up decisively in operating income ($9.4M→$69.6M). Valuation and expected return: at 8x trailing earnings, a 0.37 PEG, and 76% below the DCF, the statistical cushion is large — base case ~12-15%/yr even assuming some margin give-back, bull case 25%+/yr if the FY2025 margin holds and the pivot keeps compounding. The bear case, and this is the center of the debate: the 19% ROIC and 'Established-tier' framing lean on exactly one strong year after three years of essentially break-even operating margins (-3.5%, +0.6%, +1.4%). Gross margin barely moved (+1.6pp) while operating margin jumped nearly 7 points — that's opex leverage, not necessarily a durable pricing/mix shift, and it could reverse if NerdWallet needs to spend more on marketing to defend share against Credit Karma and Bankrate. A concentrated early holder (Topline Capital) selling ~$17.7M across three days in late June adds to the sense that this needs one more confirming data point before it's a proven story. My honest rebuttal: the valuation cushion is large enough that even a meaningful partial reversion (margin settling at 5-6% instead of 8.3%) likely still leaves the stock undervalued, the balance sheet (zero debt, strong cash) gives real staying power to wait for confirmation, and gross margin — the truest test of pricing power — has actually improved slightly, not collapsed. But 'probably fine, with real staying power' is not the same as 'confirmed durable ROIC,' and that distinction is exactly what separates a BUY from a WATCH. What to watch / when to exit: the Q2 2026 earnings call is the single most important near-term event — operating margin holding at 6%+ confirms the thesis and would justify moving back to BUY; a reversion toward 1-3% would say the FY2025 print was a one-time cost cut, and would be the trigger to walk away rather than average down.

Business: NerdWallet operates a personal-finance comparison and referral platform (credit cards, loans, insurance, banking products), monetizing when users click through to and get approved by a bank/lender partner. It is explicitly pivoting from SEO-dependent referral traffic toward higher-margin, vertically-integrated transactions.

MOAT: NARROW — one dominant source (brand/content trust and proprietary comparison data); the debate found the moat framing itself is sound, but the ROIC/'Established-tier' durability claim built on top of it is thinner than the original dossier credited moat — intangible_assets (trusted-brand content and first-party financial-comparison data built over years — 92-93% gross margin reflects the asset-light content model, and this leg has been consistently strong for four years); network_effects (more users generates more comparison data, improving lender-matching quality, though this is a softer effect than a true marketplace). Durability: 4-6. Key threat: A Google search-algorithm change is the single most credible 3-5yr threat — NerdWallet's own pivot away from SEO-dependent referrals is a direct acknowledgment of this structural vulnerability; layered on top, Credit Karma (Intuit-owned) still leads category traffic share and Bankrate (Red Ventures) dominates the highest-value mortgage/deposit queries NRDS would need to grow into to sustain its new margin profile

Bull case: The desk's Munger Small-Cap Established-tier signal is a genuine, small, high-ROIC, debt-free, accelerating business on the surface — but the debate found the 'Established' framing oversells durability: three years of near-breakeven margins were followed by exactly one strong year, driven mostly by opex leverage rather than gross-margin/mix improvement. The valuation cushion (76% below DCF, 8x earnings) is large enough to stay constructive, but this is a WATCH — a genuinely good, cheap business with one real unresolved concern — rather than a confirmed BUY until a second strong quarter shows the margin holds.

Bear case: The strongest case to avoid NRDS right now isn't the well-known Google-algorithm risk the original dossier led with — it's that the 'Established-tier, 19% ROIC' framing is built on exactly one strong year. Operating margin was -3.5%, +0.6%, and +1.4% in FY2022-2024 — essentially break-even for three straight years — before jumping to +8.3% in FY2025. Revenue grew just 22% that year, but operating income grew 7.4x; gross margin barely moved (90.8%→92.4%, +1.6pp), meaning nearly all of the margin inflection came from cutting operating expenses as a share of revenue, not from the pricing/mix story the pivot narrative implies. A screen built to find durable, multi-year ≥15% ROIC compounders has, in NRDS's case, caught a business one year removed from break-even that cut costs hard — that could be genuine operating leverage as the pivot scales, or it could be a temporary discipline push that reverses the moment renewed marketing spend is needed to defend traffic share against Credit Karma (Intuit-owned, still the largest traffic share in the category) and Bankrate (Red Ventures, dominant in the highest-value mortgage/deposit search queries). Layered on top: only 1 analyst covers the stock, and a large, concentrated holder (Topline Capital, ~1.96M shares, ~$17.7M) sold steadily across three straight days in late June 2026 — exactly the pattern of someone closer to the company than public investors heading for the exit right as the numbers turned good, even though it's a fund rather than management doing the selling.

Competitors: Credit Karma (Intuit-owned) — historically the dominant traffic leader in the personal-finance-comparison category (~46% share in the most recent detailed breakdown available), with Intuit's cross-sell/tax-data ecosystem giving it a durable acquisition-cost advantage NRDS cannot replicate. Bankrate (Red Ventures) — dominates the highest-value mortgage/deposit search queries, precisely the higher-margin comparison traffic NRDS would need to win more of to sustain its new margin profile; NerdWallet ranked second in category traffic in the most recent detailed data available (~27% share), with Bankrate a strong third and gaining. LendingTree — competes hard on large-ticket loan leads via a multi-lender bidding model that pressures the same lender-referral economics NRDS monetizes, often winning on price/conversion. Market-share trend: NRDS has been gaining traffic share over time, but Credit Karma's structural advantage (owned by Intuit, deep tax/financial data integration) and Bankrate's dominance in the highest-margin queries mean NRDS's realistic ceiling in its core comparison business may be a strong #2, not a #1. Reinvestment runway: constrained by the fact that any renewed marketing spend to defend or grow share directly reverses the very opex leverage that produced this year's ROIC — the margin story and the growth story are in tension with each other. Moat durability: NARROW, as the original dossier said, but the debate's honest read is that the 'Established-tier, 19% ROIC' framing overstates durability — this looks more like a business exiting a multi-year trough with one strong year, not a proven compounder, which argues for a more cautious 'Emerging' read even though it technically clears the Established-tier ROIC bar today. (Credit Karma/Bankrate/LendingTree competitive positioning is web-sourced; all NRDS financials are from the FMP bundle.)

Capital allocation: A- — zero debt, a real buyback (-2.9%/yr share count) funded entirely from FCF (22.0% FCF yield) rather than debt, and no management insider selling in the bundle (the only large seller, Topline Capital, is an external fund/early holder, not an executive or director). The one honest ding: with the company only one year removed from break-even, some might argue that cash should be prioritized for reinvestment (marketing/content spend to defend share) over buybacks — a minor point, not a real flag given the balance sheet strength.

Valuation: P/E (TTM) 8.0, PEG 0.37 (trailing-growth basis); DCF intrinsic value $39.70 vs price $9.58 (+76% margin of safety); Seeking Alpha (2026-06-29) independently cites 3.5x 2025 EBITDA and a $12 price-target floor; consensus price target $13.33 (range $12-15) implies ~39% upside. The valuation cushion is large enough that even a partial reversion of margin (say operating margin settling at 5-6% instead of 8.3%) likely still leaves the stock undervalued.

Margin of safety: +76% below DCF ($39.70 DCF vs $9.58 price) — real and large, which is the main reason this stays a WATCH rather than an AVOID despite the ROIC-durability concern.

Entry trigger: Q2 2026 (or Q3) results showing operating margin holding at or above ~6-7% (not reverting toward the 1-2% range of FY2023-24) while revenue growth stays at or above ~15% — that would confirm the pivot to vertically-integrated, higher-margin transactions is structural rather than a one-time opex cut, and would flip this to BUY even at a modestly higher price, given the DCF gap (76% at today's price) leaves ample room. Estimated IRR at confirmation: still ~20-25%/yr from a price modestly above today's.

Expected return (3–5y): Base ~12-15%/yr (revenue growth moderates to 12-18%, operating margin partially normalizes toward 5-6% rather than holding 8.3%, but the statistical discount still closes gradually); Bull ~25%+/yr (the SEO-to-direct-transaction pivot proves structural, FY2025's margin holds or improves, and the DCF gap closes materially); Bear -10 to 0%/yr (operating margin reverts most of the way back toward the FY2022-2024 near-breakeven range as renewed marketing spend is needed to defend traffic against Credit Karma/Bankrate, and continued large-holder selling pressures the stock). Key assumption, restated honestly: the FY2025 margin inflection is durable rather than a one-year opex-discipline event — this is the single biggest unresolved question in the thesis, not the Google-algorithm risk the original dossier led with.

What would change our mind: A Q2 2026 (or Q3) print showing operating margin holding at 6%+ while revenue growth stays double-digit would resolve the core durability question in the bull direction and justify moving back to BUY. Conversely, a reversion of operating margin back toward the 1-3% FY2023-24 range — even alongside continued revenue growth — would confirm the FY2025 inflection was a temporary opex cut rather than a structural pivot, and would argue for AVOID rather than WATCH.

Catalysts: Q2 2026 earnings call announced for a near-term date — this is now the single most important near-term event, since it will show whether the FY2025 operating-margin level (8.3%) holds or reverts; continued pivot toward vertically-integrated, higher-margin transactions; July 2026 Financial Resilience Index hit a new high (small positive brand-relevance signal).

What to watch (4–12 wks): Q2 2026 operating margin specifically — holding at or above ~6-7% (not reverting toward the 1-2% FY2023-24 range) while revenue growth stays ≥15% would be the clearest confirmation the pivot is structural; whether Topline Capital's selling continues or has concluded; any additional sell-side analyst initiations (currently just 1).

Time horizon: medium

🥊 Deep Research Memo (bull/bear debated)

🥊 Deep Research Memo (bull/bear debated)
Dlocal is a genuinely fast-growing, net-cash EM payments business: 47% revenue growth, 34% ROIC, and a DCF that says the stock is 82% too cheap. Its moat is real but narrower than a first read suggests — merchants who integrate Dlocal's compliance/API rails across ~40 emerging markets rarely re-platform, which is a legitimate switching-cost moat with 5-7 years of visible durability. But the second leg of the original bull case, pricing power from network effects, does not hold up under scrutiny: gross margin has fallen every single year for four straight years (48.3% in FY2022 to 36.8% in FY2025), and the company's own Q1 2026 disclosure (35% vs 39% a year earlier) shows the compression continuing, not stabilizing. Why now, per the original bull case: an ACI Worldwide distribution partnership just announced (2026-07-28), improving sell-side sentiment (Seeking Alpha, 2026-07-03), and a statistical discount (PEG 0.79, 19x trailing P/E) versus 47% growth. That's a real setup — if the margin trend has actually bottomed. Valuation and expected return: at $14.88 against an $81.71 DCF, the margin of safety is enormous on paper, and even a base case where growth merely holds near 25-30%/yr and margin stabilizes near current levels supports a ~15%/yr return. The bull case (~30%/yr) requires the DCF gap to actually close, which requires the margin story to turn, not just decelerate its decline. The bear case, restated plainly: DLO is winning volume by giving away margin, not by strengthening its moat, against two well-capitalized rivals (Adyen at 53-55% EBITDA margins, Stripe aggressively building EM local rails) that are closing the switching-cost gap from opposite directions. And the CEO — the person with the best visibility into whether this stabilizes — converted and sold $15.0M of stock in the first week of July, not bought. My honest rebuttal: none of this yet shows up as a broken thesis — revenue growth is accelerating, not decelerating, and the balance sheet (net cash, shrinking share count) gives real staying power to wait for margin confirmation. But "the thesis hasn't broken yet" is different from "the bear case doesn't matter," and four years of the same margin trend plus a concentrated insider sale is enough evidence, not speculation, to move this from BUY to WATCH rather than rubber-stamp the CIO's higher ranking. What to watch / when to exit: watch Q2/Q3 2026 gross margin closely — stabilization or an upward inflection off 34-36% flips this back to BUY at a very attractive IRR given the DCF gap hasn't closed. A fifth straight year of margin decline, continued insider selling from Kanovich, or a specific take-rate-compression admission on an earnings call would be reasons to exit rather than average down.

Business: Dlocal runs a cross-border payments platform connecting global merchants (it just added ACI Worldwide as a partner, announced 2026-07-28) to local payment methods across ~40 emerging markets, mainly Latin America, Africa and Asia. It earns a take rate on payment volume processed for merchants like e-commerce, streaming and gig-economy platforms operating in markets with fragmented local payment rails.

MOAT: NARROW — one clearly dominant source (switching costs from embedded integrations); after the debate the pricing-power leg looks weaker than the original dossier credited — gross margin has fallen every year for four straight years, not just "declined" per one Seeking Alpha line moat — switching_costs (merchants integrate Dlocal's API/compliance rails once and rarely re-platform across dozens of EM jurisdictions); network_effects (more merchants on the platform improves its local payment-method coverage and negotiating leverage with local banks/wallets, evidenced by 47% YoY revenue growth well above regional GDP); cost_advantage (localized licensing/compliance infrastructure across ~40 countries is expensive to replicate, supporting a still-respectable 36% gross margin). Durability: 5-7. Key threat: Stripe and Adyen are actively expanding EM/LatAm local-payment coverage; Adyen alone runs 53-55% EBITDA margins (vs. DLO's 35% gross margin in Q1 2026) while growing volume a slower but margin-accretive 8-12% — the two firms are converging on the same merchants from opposite ends of the price/margin spectrum, and DLO is the one conceding margin to hold share

Bull case: EM payments infrastructure compounder trading at a statistical discount (PEG 0.79, 82% below DCF) despite accelerating growth, but four straight years of gross-margin compression plus a concentrated $15M CEO cash-out in July are the swing factors between 'cheap' and 'value trap.'

Bear case: The strongest case to avoid DLO now is not the generic EM-payments risk list — it's that the bull thesis's own numbers show the take rate compressing every year for four straight years (gross margin 48.3% → 42.6% → 39.5% → 36.8%, FY22-FY25), with the company's own Q1 2026 print (35% vs 39% a year prior) confirming it continued this year, not stabilized. That is DLO buying revenue growth by conceding an ever-larger share of each transaction to merchants and local rails — the opposite of a strengthening moat. Layer on the CEO's own behavior: SEC filings show Sebastian Kanovich (CEO and director) converted and sold 1,025,700 shares for ~$15.0M across two trades in the first week of July 2026 alone, right as sell-side sentiment (Seeking Alpha, 2026-07-03) turned more constructive and just before a partnership headline (ACI Worldwide, 2026-07-28). The person with the best visibility into whether margin compression is ending chose that exact window to cash out, not buy. Against two well-funded rivals — Adyen running 53-55% EBITDA margins while DLO's gross margin sits at 35%, and Stripe aggressively building EM local-payment rails — the market's discount looks less like an overlooked bargain and more like a fair price for a business whose unit economics are still deteriorating.

Competitors: Adyen (AMS: ADYEN) — the most direct enterprise/EM-payments comparable. FY2025 EBITDA margin 53% (up from 50% in FY2024), H2 2025 margin 55%; processed volume grew a slower but steadier 8% in FY2025 (12% in H2). DLO's Q1 2026 gross margin was 35% (down from 39% a year earlier) on 73% TPV growth. Head-to-head: Adyen is trading margin discipline for slower growth; DLO is trading margin for faster growth — the market is pricing DLO's bigger discount precisely because that trade-off has been going the wrong way for four years running. Stripe (private) — well-capitalized, actively expanding EM/LatAm local-payment-method coverage; no public margin disclosure, but widely reported to be closing the local-rail integration gap that is DLO's core switching-cost moat. EBANX (private, Brazil-based) — a direct EM-payments peer competing for the same LatAm/Africa merchant base. Market-share trend: DLO is still gaining TPV, but via price concessions rather than pricing power — the opposite of what a durable moat should produce. Reinvestment runway: still large (EM payments infrastructure is early-innings), but current reinvestment is showing up as margin give-back, not efficiency gains. Moat durability: the switching-costs leg survives (merchants rarely re-platform); the network-effects/pricing-power leg is weaker than claimed and under active, well-funded pressure from Adyen and Stripe — this is better described as a scale/first-mover lead under erosion than a self-reinforcing network effect. (Adyen/Stripe/EBANX figures are web-sourced from company disclosures, not FMP-verified; all DLO figures are from the FMP bundle.)

Capital allocation: C+ — the buyback (-4.5%/yr share count) is real and FCF-funded (11.2% FCF yield, net cash balance sheet, no debt-funded returns), which argues for a B on its own. But capital allocation isn't just the company's official program — it's what insiders do with their own shares, and the CEO's ~$15.0M concentrated cash-out in the first week of July, timed into improving sentiment, is a real ding on insider alignment that the original dossier under-weighted by describing it as "CEO + a separate director" rather than one person's concentrated sale.

Valuation: P/E (TTM) 19.1, PEG 0.79 (forward basis); DCF intrinsic value $81.71 vs price $14.88 (+82% margin of safety); analyst consensus price target $18.50 (range $17-20) implies only modest 12-month upside despite the DCF gap — the Street's own target confirms it isn't yet crediting the DCF's implied multi-year margin recovery.

Margin of safety: +82% below DCF ($81.71 DCF vs $14.88 price) — real, but built on a DCF that assumes take-rate compression stabilizes; four years of gross-margin data plus the latest quarter argue it hasn't yet.

Entry trigger: A quarter (Q2 or Q3 2026) showing gross margin stabilizing or inflecting upward off the 34-36% range (not printing a new multi-year low), combined with no further Form 4 sales from Kanovich in the following 60 days — that combination would confirm take-rate compression has bottomed and the 82% DCF discount is a real, not a decaying, margin of safety. IRR at that point: still ~25-30%/yr from current levels given the DCF gap has not closed.

Expected return (3–5y): Base ~15%/yr (EM payment-volume growth continues near 25-30% but gross margin keeps drifting down another 200-400bps before stabilizing, capping FCF conversion); Bull ~30%/yr (take-rate compression genuinely bottoms in 2026 and the multiple re-rates toward the DCF gap); Bear -5 to 5%/yr (margin erosion continues at the current run-rate, Adyen/Stripe close more of the local-rail gap, and the insider-selling overhang caps any re-rate). Key assumption: Dlocal's local payment-method coverage keeps compounding volume faster than take-rate erodes — the trend of the last 4 years argues this assumption is not yet proven.

What would change our mind: A quarter where gross margin stops declining (holds at or above ~36-37%, or inflects up) would restore confidence that the take-rate story has stabilized and flip this back to BUY. Conversely, a fifth consecutive year of gross-margin decline, or further large Form 4 sales from Kanovich within the next two quarters, would move this toward AVOID regardless of how large the DCF discount looks on paper.

Catalysts: New ACI Worldwide global-merchant distribution partnership (announced 2026-07-28); continued Wall Street sentiment improvement noted by Seeking Alpha (2026-07-03); FY2029/2030 analyst estimates project EBITDA nearly quadrupling from current levels.

What to watch (4–12 wks): Q2/Q3 2026 gross-margin print for a genuine inflection (not just deceleration in the rate of decline) and any further Form 4 filings from Kanovich; any additional enterprise partnership wins in the ACI Worldwide vein.

💼 Goldman Sachs Small-Cap — 5 picks ▼
💼 Goldman Sachs Small-Cap
Small-cap hidden-gem scanner: $100M-$2B cap, 25%+ growth, thin coverage, insider ownership, moat, catalysts, red flags.
📖 Strategy details▼

Goldman Sachs pre-discovery screen — finding companies growing 25%+ in the $100M–$2B range before mainstream institutional flows arrive. Goal: tomorrow's $10B company at $500M today.

  • Size: $100M–$2B market cap — big enough to be legitimate, small enough to still multiply
  • Coverage: 0–5 analysts covering the stock (≥20 = already discovered)
  • Revenue growth: minimum 25% YoY for 3+ consecutive quarters
  • Insider ownership: founders/executives holding 15%+ of shares (skin in the game)
  • Structural tailwinds: AI, cybersecurity, energy transition, aging demographics, automation
  • Unit economics: improving gross margins and positive operating leverage (revenue growing faster than costs)
  • Balance sheet: 18+ months cash runway without needing profitability
  • Blindspot channels: spinoffs from S&P 500 companies, foreign listings overlooked by US investors, orphaned small-caps that fell below $500M and lost analyst coverage, post-bankruptcy equities with clean balance sheets
  • Near-term catalysts: specific re-rating events within 6–12 months (earnings beats, product launches, regulatory approvals)

🛒 Lynch Buy What You Know — 5 picks ▼
🛒 Lynch Buy What You Know
Everyday-observation → public-company mapping, classified into a Lynch category with a valuation sanity check.
📖 Strategy details▼

Peter Lynch's everyday-life observation framework. Simple, understandable consumer and workplace businesses growing 15–25%/yr at PEG <1.0. The best investments hide in plain sight — find them before Wall Street does.

  • Daily life inventory: products, apps, or services you're using more this year than last year
  • Emerging behaviour patterns: what friends, family, and colleagues are doing differently than 2 years ago
  • Workplace intelligence: what tools or software your company is buying or switching to
  • Kids' trends: products and brands teenagers are obsessed with that parents haven't noticed yet
  • Retail observation: which stores have lines, which brands are sold out, what everyone is talking about
  • Lynch category: classify each as Fast Grower (20%+ growth), Stalwart, Cyclical, Turnaround, or Asset Play
  • The 'so what' test: a popular product doesn't automatically make a great stock — always check valuation and fundamentals

💯 Mayer 100-Bagger — 3 picks ▼
💯 Mayer 100-Bagger
Small cap + high ROIC + owner-operator + long runway — the 100-bagger checklist. May return zero picks.
📖 Strategy details▼

Christopher Mayer's 100-Bagger framework — the research methodology identifying stocks with potential to return 100x, based on patterns observed across 365 historical 100-baggers.

  • Small starting cap: ideally under $1B — 100x must be mathematically possible
  • Long runway: serves a market large enough to support decades of revenue growth
  • ROIC above 20%: Mayer's single most predictive metric — the engine of compounding
  • Earnings growth: 20%+ annual earnings growth sustained for many years
  • Owner-operator: CEO and management with 10%+ personal stock ownership
  • Reinvestment runway: profits redeployed into new growth at high returns (not paid out as dividends)
  • No dilution: the company isn't issuing large amounts of new shares that erode long-term returns
  • Twin engines test: can earnings grow 10x AND the P/E multiple also expand to compound into 100x?
  • Time horizon reality: 100-baggers typically take 20–25 years — patience is the edge

🔢 Greenblatt Magic Formula — 10 picks ▼
🔢 Greenblatt Magic Formula
ROIC>20% + earnings yield>10% ranked screen, ex-financials/utilities/REITs. Top 10, not a curated shortlist.
📖 Strategy details▼

Joel Greenblatt's Magic Formula — the two-factor screen generating 30%+ annual returns over 20 years by finding companies that are simultaneously high-quality AND cheap.

  • ROIC above 20%: high-quality business generating strong returns on every dollar invested
  • Earnings yield above 10%: cheap relative to earnings (inverse of P/E) — the 'cheap' gate
  • Combined ranking: companies score best when BOTH metrics rank highly — quality + cheap together
  • Size filter: $50M–$10B to exclude illiquid micro-caps and already-covered mega-caps
  • Sector exclusions: skip financials, utilities, and REITs (different capital structures distort the formula)
  • Debt check: high ROIC shouldn't be mere financial leverage — verify balance sheet is clean
  • Earnings quality: free cash flow should match net income — flag accounting-driven earnings
  • Temporary vs permanent: is the stock cheap due to a fixable problem, or is the business structurally declining?

🎲 Pabrai Asymmetric Bet — 3 picks ▼
🎲 Pabrai Asymmetric Bet
3:1+ upside/downside bets with explicit downside protection — distress, special situations, hated industries.
📖 Strategy details▼

Mohnish Pabrai's Dhandho framework — combining LOW RISK (limited downside) with HIGH UNCERTAINTY (Wall Street can't value it) for asymmetric bets where heads I win big, tails I don't lose much.

  • Asymmetry ratio: upside potential ÷ downside risk must be 3:1 or better
  • Downside protection: what specifically limits the loss — asset value, cash, acquisition target, recurring revenue
  • Upside catalyst: the specific event that could drive 3–10x returns over 3–5 years
  • Temporary distress: markets treating a short-term problem (lawsuit, earnings miss, sector rotation) as permanent
  • Special situations: spinoffs, post-bankruptcy equities, rights offerings that create pricing inefficiencies
  • Hated industries: entire sectors abandoned by investors where survivors trade at distressed multiples
  • Margin of safety: gap between current price and conservative intrinsic value — the buffer against being wrong

🔄 Marks Second-Level — 5 picks ▼
🔄 Marks Second-Level
Consensus audit + second-level question — oversold/overbought extremes, narrative-vs-numbers gaps.
📖 Strategy details▼

Howard Marks' second-level thinking — first-level thinking gets average returns; second-level thinking ('the company is great BUT priced for perfection') finds the real opportunities.

  • Consensus audit: what is the mainstream view, and is it based on sound analysis or herd mentality?
  • Second-level question: what do I know or see that the consensus is missing?
  • Oversold opportunities: stocks down 50%+ where the negative narrative has become excessive vs fundamentals
  • Sentiment extremes: sectors at multi-year sentiment lows (rare to be wrong buying) or highs (rare to be right buying)
  • Narrative vs numbers gap: where does the market story ('this industry is dying') contradict the actual data?
  • Time horizon arbitrage: quarterly-focused Wall Street missing a multi-year thesis
  • Insider buying signal: executives aggressively buying when the market is selling — the strongest bullish insider indicator

🌀 Sleep Scale Economics Shared — 5 picks ▼
🌀 Sleep Scale Economics Shared
Businesses that share scale economics with customers via a reinforcing flywheel and long-term management.
📖 Strategy details▼

Nick Sleep's Scale Economics Shared framework — the methodology that identified Amazon, Costco, and Berkshire decades early, based on companies that share their scale advantages with customers to build a self-reinforcing flywheel.

  • Core test: does the company get MORE efficient and offer BETTER prices as it grows? (opposite of most businesses)
  • Customer obsession: willing to take short-term margin hits to give customers more value (Costco 15% margin discipline)
  • Flywheel: lower prices → more customers → more scale → lower costs → even lower prices (self-reinforcing loop)
  • Long-term thinking evidence: quarterly earnings suppressed for multi-year investment; founder letters emphasise decades
  • Customer lifetime value: expanding over time as the business creates more value per customer
  • Non-obvious moat: the advantage isn't patents or brand — it's a culture and business model the organisation embodies
  • Capital allocation: cash flow reinvested into high-return opportunities rather than buybacks at peak prices

🕳️ Burry Catalyst Deep Value — 5 picks ▼
🕳️ Burry Catalyst Deep Value
Hidden assets, sum-of-the-parts, activist/regulatory catalysts — each with an explicit timeline.
📖 Strategy details▼

Michael Burry's catalyst-driven deep value approach — finding mispriced assets where specific, identifiable catalysts will force the market to recognise hidden value within a defined timeframe.

  • Hidden assets: companies trading below the value of real estate, cash, or investments on the balance sheet
  • Sum-of-parts: conglomerates where individual divisions are worth more than the combined market cap
  • Activist catalyst: stocks where an activist could force a spinoff, sale, or restructuring to unlock value
  • Regulatory / legal catalysts: upcoming court cases or policy decisions that will materially reprice the stock
  • Balance sheet transformation: companies paying down debt aggressively — will re-rate once leverage drops below key thresholds
  • Accounting normalisation: one-time write-downs or unusual items temporarily depressing reported earnings
  • Catalyst timeline: each idea must have a specific catalyst with 6–18 month resolution — no 'cheap forever' open-ended theses

🛰️ Wall Street Blindspot — 5 picks ▼
🛰️ Wall Street Blindspot
Coverage-gap hunting — foreign listings, spinoffs, orphaned small-caps, sin-stock discounts — as a prioritized workflow.
📖 Strategy details▼

Wall Street Blindspot framework — finding investment opportunities that major banks structurally cannot or will not cover: coverage gaps, orphaned names, stigmatised sectors, complex structures.

  • Coverage gap: companies with 0–5 sell-side analysts — institutions only cover above $2B, leaving quality names persistently mispriced
  • Orphaned mid-caps: companies that fell below $500M and lost coverage — often trading at deep discounts to intrinsic value
  • Spinoff aftermath: newly independent companies facing forced selling from index funds in the first 18 months
  • Sin-sector discounts: quality companies in gambling, tobacco, fossil fuels, or defence at persistent ESG mandate discounts
  • Post-bankruptcy emergence: restructured balance sheets institutional investors can't own due to mandate restrictions
  • IPO aftermath: quality companies 18–24 months post-IPO when lockup expiry creates selling pressure
  • Key signal: the discount reason is structural or temporary, not fundamental — the business is better than the price suggests

💼 Goldman Sachs Small-Cap▼ full report
GOLDMAN SACHS SMALL-CAP HIDDEN GEM SCANNER -- Desk Note, July 29, 2026 Coverage universe for this note: $100M-$2B market cap, 25%+ revenue growth sustained across multiple quarters, 0-5 sell-side analysts, and where obtainable, 15%+ insider ownership. All hard financials (market cap, margins, ROIC, growth, FCF yield, analyst-count) are pulled from the FMP-sourced candidate metrics_block in desk_input.json -- no invented figures. Insider-ownership percentages, which FMP's compact metrics_block does not carry, were pulled via web search (WallStreetZen, GuruFocus, Simply Wall St, company Form 4 filings) dated July 2026 and are flagged explicitly below each name. --- 1) INNOVATIVE SOLUTIONS AND SUPPORT, INC. (ISSC) Growth: Revenue +79% YoY, accelerating from +36% the prior year; 5yr CAGR 28%. Coverage: 1 sell-side analyst -- essentially uncovered. Insider Ownership: 55.05% per WallStreetZen/GuruFocus (web-sourced, not FMP) -- one of the highest insider stakes we've screened this cycle, plus 48.9% institutional overlap suggesting long-only funds are quietly accumulating alongside management. Tailwinds: FAA-driven cockpit-avionics modernization cycle on aging business-jet and regional-airline fleets, plus a defense-adjacent flight-data/display angle that keeps this out of pure-commercial cyclicality. Unit Economics: 49% gross margin, 25% operating margin, both consistent with a business gaining operating leverage as volume scales on a fixed engineering base. Balance Sheet: FCF yield 4.0% and no debt-distress signal in the metrics_block; management has historically run this shop debt-light. Moat: certification/patent-protected avionics designs plus multi-year OEM qualification cycles are real switching costs -- a new entrant can't just show up with a cheaper box. Catalysts (6-12mo): (i) additional STC (supplemental type certificate) wins on new aircraft platforms, (ii) potential defense/counter-UAS avionics contract award, (iii) initiation by a second sell-side house given the growth inflection. Red Flag: at a $343M market cap with 79% growth, the name is thinly traded -- a single large holder exiting could move the stock more than the fundamentals justify, and PEG-basis valuation already prices in a lot of continued acceleration. Verdict: BUY-the-dip candidate; the insider-ownership signal here is about as clean as this screen produces. 2) VINCI COMPASS INVESTMENTS LTD. (VINP) Growth: Revenue +44% YoY, accelerating from +18%; 5yr CAGR 39%. Coverage: 4 analysts (still thin for an asset manager of this AUM scale). Insider Ownership: 43% per Simply Wall St (web-sourced) -- founders Manuel Balbontin and Jaime de la Barra (Compass) rolled substantially all of their stake into the combined Vinci entity, which is the kind of skin-in-the-game a pure US wealth manager rarely offers retail investors access to. Tailwinds: LatAm (primarily Brazilian and Chilean) private-wealth and alternatives penetration is still single-digit as a % of investable assets vs. 25%+ in developed markets -- multi-decade AUM-gathering runway. Unit Economics: 80% gross margin typical of an asset-light fee business; operating margin still modest at 9%, meaning there's real operating leverage left to unlock as AUM scales against a largely fixed cost base. Balance Sheet: FCF yield 6.1%, DCF margin of safety +84% per the FMP model (though note DCF models are a blunt instrument for AUM-based fee businesses -- treat as directional, not precise). Moat: relationship-based distribution network across LatAm private banks plus multi-year lock-ups on alternatives products. Catalysts: (i) further AUM inflows as Brazilian rates ease, (ii) US ADR liquidity improving as index inclusion becomes plausible, (iii) potential bolt-on M&A given a public currency. Red Flag: share count +11.6%/yr -- this is a dilution story as much as a growth story, and EM asset-manager multiples get crushed fast in a risk-off tape. Verdict: BUY for investors comfortable with EM/Brazil currency and political risk; size smaller than ISSC. 3) EXZEO GROUP, INC. (XZO) Growth: Revenue +62% YoY, accelerating from +52%. Coverage: 2 analysts. Insider Ownership: direct CEO (Paresh Patel) ownership is modest in share count, but parent HCI Group retains ~81.5% post-IPO per web research (StockTitan, InsNerds) -- effectively this is a controlled subsidiary, not a widely-held small cap, and Patel has been buying in the open market post-IPO as a confidence signal. Tailwinds: a hardening Florida (and broadening multi-state) homeowners-insurance market where legacy carriers have pulled back, creating share-gain runway for a tech-native MGA/insurtech platform. Unit Economics: 56% gross margin, 45% operating margin -- genuinely excellent for an insurance-adjacent business, reflecting a capital-light fee/MGA model rather than full risk retention. Balance Sheet: FCF yield 8.5%, 3 insider buys totaling $82K in the disclosed period. Moat: proprietary underwriting/pricing technology plus the parent's decades of Florida-specific claims data is a real cost advantage vs. a de novo entrant. Catalysts: (i) geographic expansion beyond Florida, (ii) hurricane-season reinsurance renewal pricing (a swing factor both ways), (iii) further parent-company monetization/spin-down that could re-rate the float. Red Flag: single-state (originally) catastrophe concentration -- one bad hurricane season tests the whole thesis, and the controlling parent stake means minority shareholders have limited influence over capital-allocation decisions. Verdict: WATCH-to-BUY; wants a clean hurricane season as the near-term catalyst. 4) PAGAYA TECHNOLOGIES LTD. (PGY) Growth: Revenue +26% YoY, decelerating from +30% -- still comfortably above the 25% bar but the trend line is the one thing to watch. Coverage: 2 analysts. Insider Ownership: web sources disagree (14.75% to 42% depending on definition of "insider"), but CEO stock purchases (16,230 shares recently, per Yahoo Finance) are a positive tell regardless of which number you trust. Tailwinds: AI-based credit underwriting displacing legacy FICO-only decisioning across bank and fintech partners -- point-of-sale and auto lending are the next expansion legs beyond personal loans. Unit Economics: 41% gross margin, 22% operating margin, FCF yield an eye-catching 18.8%. Balance Sheet: no debt-distress flag; the funding-partner network model means Pagaya doesn't carry the loans on its own balance sheet, which de-risks the credit cycle exposure relative to a traditional lender. Moat: network effects between funding partners (asset managers/insurers) and origination partners (banks/fintechs) -- more of one attracts more of the other. Catalysts: (i) new asset-class expansion (auto, POS), (ii) additional bank-partner signings, (iii) a credit-cycle "soft landing" validating the underwriting models live. Red Flag: share count +10.5%/yr -- warrant/earnout dilution from the de-SPAC structure remains a real drag on per-share value creation even as the business itself is decelerating-but-real growth. Verdict: BUY for investors who trust the credit models through a cycle; the dilution is the thing keeping this out of HIGH conviction. 5) TELOS CORPORATION (TLS) Growth: Revenue +52% YoY, a sharp acceleration off a prior -26% decline -- this is the riskiest, most turnaround-flavored name on the list, included because the growth reacceleration is real and coverage is essentially zero (1 analyst). Insider Ownership: web sources range 7%-16% (ChartMill vs. TipRanks) -- notably lower than the other four names here, and recent Form 4s show director Bradley Jacobs selling shares, which cuts against the thesis. Tailwinds: federal zero-trust cybersecurity mandates and continued government IT-modernization spend are real and multi-year. Unit Economics: gross margin 36%, but operating margin is still -8% -- this business has not yet proven it can convert federal contract wins into GAAP profitability. Balance Sheet: FCF yield 8.0% (better than the margin line suggests, likely working-capital driven -- verify durability). Moat: security clearances and federal supplier accreditation are real switching-cost moats once won, but Telos has to actually win and hold the contracts first. Catalysts: (i) further federal budget releases for zero-trust initiatives, (ii) a follow-on contract award validating the growth reacceleration, (iii) a path to op-margin breakeven that would re-rate the stock. Red Flag, and it's the single biggest one on this entire list: negative operating margin and negative ROIC despite the revenue reacceleration, combined with an insider (not a random employee -- a board-level name) selling into the print. This is a "prove it" story, not yet a "hidden gem." Verdict: WATCH only -- would need a clean profitable quarter before sizing this as a real position.
🛒 Lynch Buy What You Know▼ full report
PETER LYNCH -- BUY WHAT YOU KNOW, Fieldwork Notes, July 29, 2026 A quick disclosure up front: all five names below are FMP-verified pool candidates -- every hard number (P/E, PEG, ROIC, margins, revenue growth, DCF margin of safety) comes straight from the desk's metrics_block, not from memory or a web guess. The "everyday observation" that sparked each idea is my own fieldwork/training-knowledge framing, but the numbers behind the "so-what test" are real. This is the good version of buy-what-you-know: the observation gets you looking, the financials decide whether you buy. --- DUOLINGO (DUOL) -- [Fast Grower] The observation: you cannot get through a subway car or a waiting room anymore without seeing someone poke at that green owl app for their two-minute streak. My own nephew set an alarm so he wouldn't lose a 400-day streak. That's not a fad, that's a habit loop, and habit loops are exactly what make a consumer app investable rather than just popular. Category: this is a straightforward Fast Grower -- revenue is up 39% year over year, and the five-year trend line shows this isn't a one-quarter blip (20% five-year CAGR with the growth rate stable-to-accelerating). The so-what test: a Fast Grower at 39% revenue growth "ought" to command a rich multiple, but Duolingo trades at 11.8x trailing earnings with a PEG of just 0.66 and the FMP DCF model pegs a 69% margin of safety to intrinsic value. When the popular product AND the valuation both say buy, that's the Lynch sweet spot. Watch the operating margin (15%) for continued improvement as the subscription mix (Super Duolingo, the streak-freeze upsell) scales against a mostly-fixed content-production cost base. DECKERS OUTDOOR (DECK) -- [Fast Grower / Stalwart hybrid] The observation: I used to think Hoka was a niche ultramarathoner thing. Now it's on every third pair of feet at my gym, my dentist wears them, and the local running-shoe store has a whole wall for them next to the UGG boots that, somehow, never went out of style with a certain demographic either. When a company owns two brands at completely different points in the fashion cycle -- one still hyper-growth (Hoka), one a durable stalwart (UGG) -- that diversification is underappreciated by a market that still mentally files Deckers as "that boot company." Category: Fast Grower, tilting Stalwart as Hoka's growth normalizes. The numbers: revenue +16% YoY, ROIC an excellent 33%, and -- this is the part Lynch would circle twice -- 14.2x trailing earnings with a PEG of 1.45 and +44% margin of safety to DCF fair value, while management is aggressively buying back stock (+7.2%/yr buyback yield, shrinking share count). So-what test: passes cleanly. This is a real business, growing at a real rate, at a price that isn't demanding you believe in a miracle. MERCADOLIBRE (MELI) -- [Fast Grower] The observation: every person I know with family in Argentina, Brazil, or Mexico either shops on this, banks on this (Mercado Pago), or both. It is genuinely "the Amazon and PayPal of Latin America" and I don't say that as a lazy comp -- it's functionally true for a few hundred million people. Category: unambiguous Fast Grower, revenue +39% YoY, stable at a 22% five-year CAGR. So-what test: this is where buy-what-you-know needs its cold shower. At 44x trailing earnings, the stock trades at a PEG of 0.94 (fine) but the FMP DCF model shows a -173% margin of safety -- meaning the price is roughly two-and-a-half times the model's fair-value estimate. A great business everyone already knows about is not automatically a good stock at any price, and MELI's ubiquity in daily conversation cuts both ways: Wall Street already has this one figured out. MEDIUM conviction -- own it for the growth durability, size it knowing you're paying up. NOVO NORDISK (NOVO-B.CO) -- [Stalwart] The observation: this is the one where "buy what you know" almost writes itself and that's exactly why I want to slow down. Everyone is talking about Ozempic and Wegovy -- at family dinners, in the news, in the group chat. If ever there were a "the whole world is suddenly using this" signal, GLP-1 drugs are it. Category: Stalwart -- this is a $217B, large, mature pharma business, not a scrappy Fast Grower, even though the underlying drug class is genuinely revolutionary. So-what test, and this is the important part: revenue growth has decelerated hard, from 25% two years ago to just 6% now, competitive pressure (Eli Lilly's Zepbound, oral GLP-1 entrants, compounding-pharmacy competition) is real, and the FMP DCF model shows a -62% margin of safety -- the stock is priced well above the model's fair value even after this year's pullback. This is the textbook Lynch cautionary tale: the product being everywhere in daily life told you about a real secular trend two or three years ago, but by the time it's dinner-table conversation, the valuation has usually already run past what the fundamentals can cleanly support, and the growth deceleration here confirms competition is arriving. LOW-MEDIUM conviction -- I'd want a real valuation reset (or confirmation the deceleration is bottoming) before adding meaningfully.

MAYER100X — THE 100-BAGGER FRAMEWORK, APPLIED TO TODAY'S POOL Christopher Mayer's "100 Baggers" is a rigor filter, not an idea generator — the framework kills far more names than it passes, and that is the entire point of running it faithfully. Applied against today's ~100-name candidate pool (metrics_block only, no live --fetch calls), the seven-criteria screen is brutal: small starting market cap, a long growth runway, ROIC 15-20%+, 20%+ annual earnings-growth potential, an owner-operator with 10%+ personal skin in the game, high-return reinvestment optionality, a durable moat, no heavy dilution, and finally the "twin engines" test — can earnings realistically grow 10x AND can the multiple re-rate on top of that? Given the desk's own track record on this persona is the softest of the four in this batch (n=25, alpha +5.3%, win 56% — barely a coin-flip), the right response is more selectivity, not less. Three names cleared enough of the seven gates to be worth writing up; dozens of small-cap names in the pool were screened and rejected below. WHY SO FEW SURVIVE Scanning the sub-$2B names in the pool for ROIC>15% AND revenue growth accelerating AND minimal dilution eliminates almost everything immediately: PAYS (ROIC 13%, fails), MNTN (ROIC 13%, fails), USNA/NATR/GNE/TXO/BWMN/ALLT/TLS/KRNT (all ROIC under 15% or negative), BH (ROIC 3%), ALKT (ROIC -6%, actively unprofitable at the operating line despite 33% growth). AGCC (Agencia Comercial Spirits) posted a startling 186% revenue growth figure with 38% ROIC, but with no P/E, no analyst coverage and a -0.1% FCF yield in the metrics_block, there simply isn't enough verifiable data to clear Mayer's bar — a 100-bagger thesis has to survive scrutiny, not require faith, so it's excluded rather than reached for. ABUS (Arbutus Biopharma) posted ROIC 57% and revenue growth 128%, but FCF yield is -4.1% against dilution of +3.2%/yr — the earnings are almost certainly royalty/litigation-driven and not representative of a repeatable operating engine, so it fails the "high-return reinvestment" and "durable moat" tests even though the headline numbers look like a screen-topper. That is exactly the kind of number that a less disciplined process would chase; Mayer's framework exists to say no to it. Sonar/subsea sensor technology has real switching costs and specification lock-in with subsea/oil-services customers, but the company's diversification into EV electronics dilutes the "one deep moat" story into several shallower ones. - No heavy dilution: PASS. A PE of 25.8 is not yet cheap, so most of the return has to come from the earnings engine (10x on 43%-and-accelerating growth is a real, if optimistic, possibility over 8-10 years) rather than multiple expansion — that's a normal, not a red-flag, sequencing for a 100-bagger candidate this early. VERDICT: Best combined-criteria name in the pool. 100-bagger probability: LOW-MEDIUM (call it a "long-shot with real evidence behind it" rather than a high-conviction call) — the moat is the weak link, and starting cap is already a notch above ideal. 2) ELECTROMED, INC. A screen that passes every numeric gate but fails the moat test is a textbook false positive for this framework. BOTTOM LINE Zero HIGH-conviction 100-bagger candidates in today's pool — consistent with the framework's own selectivity and with this persona's middling historical alpha, which argues for tightening the bar further rather than reaching to fill a quota. NORBT.OL is the most complete story but starts above the ideal size band with a diffuse moat; ELMD is the cleanest quality name but the growth engine is a step too slow; NRDS has the numbers but fails the single most important non-numeric test in the framework. The three ideas below are all sourced from exactly the categories the framework points to — a hated/abandoned commodity industry, a sin-stock discount, and an emerging-market discount on a business with a clear multi-year catalyst — rather than from generic "cheap stock" screening. The floor is the balance sheet, not the income statement: management has been buying back stock (net buyback yield +2.6%/yr) and an insider bought $2.84M of stock at current depressed prices — a real, dated signal that people closest to the business see the current price as below liquidation/replacement value of the reserve base. DCF margin of safety of +68% (even on trailing-depressed earnings) reinforces that the market is pricing this as a structurally dying business rather than a cyclical trough. Upside catalyst (3-5yr): Met (metallurgical) coal is a steel-making input with no large-scale substitute at commercial scale yet; any recovery in global infrastructure/steel capex (or a met-coal supply-side shakeout as ESG pressure forces marginal competitors to shut down first) would swing AMR's earnings from trough to mid-cycle rapidly given its operating leverage. Asymmetry: at a price implying continued -28%-style revenue decline in perpetuity, versus a plausible mid-cycle recovery scenario, a 3:1+ setup is defensible — downside is "reserves are worth close to today's market cap even in a bad case," upside is "a normal met-coal cycle recovery re-rates this multiples higher." Position sizing: SMALL, 3-4% of a Pabrai-style asymmetric sleeve — commodity cyclicals can stay depressed longer than the thesis survives, and coal-specific ESG-driven capital-flight risk is structural, not just sentiment, so this is sized for "high asymmetry, meaningfully lower certainty" rather than a core holding. 2) SCANDINAVIAN TOBACCO GROUP A/S (STG.CO) — Denmark, Consumer Defensive/Tobacco, mkt cap $819M Downside protection: Tobacco (specifically cigars/pipe tobacco here, a hated-industry discount layered on top of the general tobacco stigma discount) trades at a P/E of 8.8 with an FCF yield of 10.7% — the cash generation alone provides a real income floor, and the DCF margin of safety is +35%.
